subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 10. In this unit you will become confident and fluent with percentages – one of the most useful ideas in all of mathematics. A percentage is simply a way of describing a part of something out of one hundred, and once you see how it works you will notice percentages everywhere. When Amina compares two market stalls in Hargeisa to find the bigger discount, when Yusuf works out how much interest his savings will earn, or when Halima checks whether a trader made a fair profit selling goats, they are all using percentages.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics 0862 — Stage 8 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Calculate a percentage of an amount quickly using decimals, fractions and mental methods.
Find a percentage change using the formula change ÷ original × 100%.
Increase or decrease an amount using a multiplier (for example ×1.15 or ×0.85).
Solve reverse percentage problems to find the original amount before a change.
Calculate simple interest using Interest = Principal × Rate × Time.
Work out profit and loss as a percentage of the cost price.
Apply percentages to real problems: discounts, tax, tips, savings and trade.

concepts.title: Finding a Percentage of an Amount
concepts.explanation:
Everything in this unit builds on one core skill: finding a percentage of an amount. There are three reliable methods, and a strong mathematician chooses the quickest one for each problem. Let us look at all three, because being able to switch between them is what makes you fast and accurate.

Method 1 – the decimal method. Turn the percentage into a decimal by dividing by 100, then multiply. To find 30% of 80: 30% = 0.30, and 0.30 × 80 = 24. To find 15% of 240: 15% = 0.15, and 0.15 × 240 = 36. This method works for any percentage and is the one to reach for when you have a calculator.

Method 2 – the fraction method. Some percentages are friendly fractions. Because 25% = 1/4, finding 25% of 120 is just 120 ÷ 4 = 30. Because 50% = 1/2, we halve; because 10% = 1/10, we divide by 10. To find 60% of 150, use 60% = 3/5: (3 × 150) ÷ 5 = 450 ÷ 5 = 90. When the fraction is simple, this is often the fastest route of all.

Method 3 – the building-block method (1% and 10%). Find an easy piece first, then build up. To find 17% of 300: first 1% of 300 = 3, so 17% = 17 × 3 = 51. To find 45% of 160 using 10% blocks: 10% of 160 = 16, so 40% = 4 × 16 = 64, and 5% is half of 16 = 8, giving 45% = 64 + 8 = 72. This method is wonderful for mental arithmetic in the market, where Sahra can work out a discount in her head without any calculator.
concepts.example: Let us gather the most useful mental shortcuts in one place, because knowing these by heart will speed up everything you do. To find 50%, divide by 2. To find 25%, divide by 4. To find 20%, divide by 5. To find 10%, divide by 10. To find 5%, find 10% then halve it. To find 1%, divide by 100. For example, 20% of 85 shillings is 85 ÷ 5 = 17 shillings, and 5% of 240 is (240 ÷ 10) ÷ 2 = 24 ÷ 2 = 12. Practise these until they feel automatic.

concepts.title: Percentage Increase and Decrease
concepts.explanation:
Very often a quantity does not stay still – it goes up or down. A price rises, a population grows, a discount lowers a cost. To find the new amount, you have two good methods, and it is worth knowing both.

Method A – find the change, then add or subtract. To increase $60 by 25%: first find 25% of $60 = 0.25 × 60 = $15, then add it on: $60 + $15 = $75. To decrease 80 kg by 15%: find 15% of 80 = 12 kg, then subtract: 80 − 12 = 68 kg. This method shows clearly *how much* the change is, which is helpful when a problem asks for the change itself.

Method B – use a multiplier. This is faster and is the professional way to do it. A multiplier is a single decimal that does the whole job in one multiplication. For an increase, you multiply by (100% + increase), written as a decimal. A 25% increase means multiplying by 100% + 25% = 125% = 1.25. So $60 × 1.25 = $75 – the same answer in one step. For a decrease, you multiply by (100% − decrease). A 15% decrease means 100% − 15% = 85% = 0.85, so 80 × 0.85 = 68 kg.

Understanding *why* the multiplier works is important, so let us think it through. When you increase something by 25%, the new amount is the whole original (which is 100% of itself) plus another 25%, making 125% of the original altogether. And 125% written as a decimal is 1.25. When you decrease by 15%, you keep 100% − 15% = 85% of the original, and 85% as a decimal is 0.85. So the multiplier is never a mystery – it is simply the percentage of the original that you end up keeping.
concepts.example: Here are the multipliers you will use most. A +10% change uses ×1.10; +25% uses ×1.25; +50% uses ×1.50; +100% uses ×2.0 (doubling). Going down, −10% uses ×0.90; −25% uses ×0.75; −50% uses ×0.50 (halving). Notice a lovely pattern: an increase multiplier is always more than 1, and a decrease multiplier is always less than 1. If you ever write a decrease multiplier bigger than 1, you know at once you have made a slip.

concepts.title: Calculating Percentage Change
concepts.explanation:
Sometimes you are told the old value and the new value, and you must work out the percentage change between them. There is one formula for this, and it is worth learning by heart:

Percentage change = (change ÷ original amount) × 100%

The two things to be careful about are: first, the change is the difference between the new and old values; and second, you always divide by the original (the starting value), never by the new one. Choosing the wrong number on the bottom of the fraction is the single most common mistake in this whole topic, so pause and ask yourself every time: which value did we start from?

Example of an increase. A trader's daily earnings rise from $80 to $92. The change is $92 − $80 = $12. The original is $80. So the percentage increase = (12 ÷ 80) × 100% = 0.15 × 100% = 15%. Notice we divided by 80, the amount we started with.

Example of a decrease. The price of a bag of rice falls from $120 to $96. The change is $120 − $96 = $24. The original is $120. So the percentage decrease = (24 ÷ 120) × 100% = 0.20 × 100% = 20%. Again we divided by the starting value, 120.
concepts.example: This same formula answers the question *what percentage is one number of another?* To ask what percentage 15 is of 60, you compute (15 ÷ 60) × 100% = 25%. Hassan uses exactly this when he works out that scoring 42 out of 120 marks in a test is (42 ÷ 120) × 100% = 35%. Whenever you see the words *out of*, think of this division followed by × 100%.

concepts.title: Reverse Percentage Problems
concepts.explanation:
This is one of the most powerful ideas in the unit, and one that trips up many learners – so read it slowly. In a reverse percentage problem you are told the amount *after* a change, and you must find the original amount from before the change. The secret is to think in multipliers and then divide by the multiplier instead of multiplying.

Here is the key idea. Going forwards, we do: original × multiplier = new amount. So going backwards we must do the opposite of multiplying, which is dividing: original = new amount ÷ multiplier. That single sentence unlocks every reverse-percentage question.

Example – after an increase. After a 20% pay rise, Omar's monthly salary is now $36,000. What was it before? A 20% increase uses the multiplier 1.2, so original × 1.2 = 36,000. To reverse it, divide: original = 36,000 ÷ 1.2 = $30,000. Check it forwards: $30,000 × 1.2 = $36,000. Correct.

Example – after a discount. In a Mogadishu shop a jacket is reduced by 15% and now costs $68. What was the original price? A 15% discount uses the multiplier 0.85, so original × 0.85 = 68. Reverse it: original = 68 ÷ 0.85 = $80. Check forwards: $80 × 0.85 = $68. Correct.
concepts.example: The biggest error here is to find 20% or 15% of the *final* amount and add or subtract it. That is wrong, because the percentage was taken from the original amount, not the new one. For instance, 15% of the $68 sale price is not the discount – the discount was 15% of the unknown original $80. Always set up original × multiplier = new amount, then divide. And always check your answer by working forwards again.

concepts.title: Simple Interest
concepts.explanation:
When you save money in a bank, the bank pays you extra money for keeping it there – this reward is called interest. When you borrow money, you pay interest instead. In this unit we study simple interest, which is the most straightforward kind: the interest is worked out only on the original amount you saved, called the principal, and it is the same every year.

The formula is short and worth memorising:

Interest = Principal × Rate × Time, often written I = P × R × T.

Here the rate must be written as a decimal (so 5% becomes 0.05), and the time is measured in years. The interest you find is the *extra* money earned; to get the total amount in the account, you add the interest back onto the principal.

Example. Ibrahim saves a principal of $1,000 at a rate of 5% per year for 3 years. Interest = 1,000 × 0.05 × 3 = $150. So over three years he earns $150 of interest, and the total in his account is $1,000 + $150 = $1,150. Notice that with simple interest he earns the same $50 each year (1,000 × 0.05), three years in a row, making $150.
concepts.example: A second example. Khadija puts $500 into a savings account at 4% simple interest for 2 years. Interest = 500 × 0.04 × 2 = $40, and the total amount is $500 + $40 = $540. You can also reverse this idea: if $800 grows to $920 in one year, the interest earned is $120, and the rate is (120 ÷ 800) × 100% = 15% – which is just our percentage-change formula in a new costume.

concepts.title: Profit and Loss
concepts.explanation:
Trade is at the heart of daily life, from the camel markets of Garissa to the shops of Eastleigh. Anyone who buys goods to sell them again needs to understand profit and loss. The cost price is what an item cost to buy or make; the selling price is what it is sold for. If the selling price is higher, there is a profit; if it is lower, there is a loss.

To express profit or loss as a percentage, we use our percentage-change idea, and by convention we compare against the cost price:

Percentage profit = (profit ÷ cost price) × 100%, and likewise for loss.

Example – profit. A craftsman makes a stool for a cost price of $40 and sells it for $60. The profit is $60 − $40 = $20. So the percentage profit = (20 ÷ 40) × 100% = 50%. He made a 50% profit on what it cost him.

Example – loss. A trader buys a sack of mangoes for $50 but, because some spoil, sells the rest for only $42. The loss is $50 − $42 = $8. The percentage loss = (8 ÷ 50) × 100% = 16%. Notice again that we divide by the cost price, the amount the trader started with.
concepts.example: This connects neatly with business ideas you will meet later. A shop with revenue of $50,000 and costs of $35,000 has a profit of $15,000, and a profit margin of (15,000 ÷ 50,000) × 100% = 30% – though margins are usually measured against revenue rather than cost, so always read carefully which base a question wants. For this unit, unless told otherwise, profit and loss percentages are taken on the cost price.

methods.title: How to find a percentage of an amount
steps: Turn the percentage into a decimal by dividing by 100.
Multiply the decimal by the amount.
Use a friendly fraction (such as 1/4 for 25%) or 10%-building-blocks as a quick check.
Write the answer with the correct units.

methods.title: How to increase an amount by a percentage
steps: Write the multiplier: 1 + p (for example, +8% gives 1.08).
Multiply the original amount by the multiplier.
Check the answer is larger than the amount you started with.
Check by parts: find the percentage separately and add it on.

methods.title: How to decrease an amount by a percentage
steps: Write the multiplier: 1 − p (for example, −12% gives 0.88).
Multiply the original amount by the multiplier.
Check the answer is smaller than the amount you started with.
Check by parts: find the percentage separately and subtract it.

methods.title: Percentage change
methods.example: A shopkeeper's weekly revenue rises from $800,000 to $920,000. Find the percentage increase.
steps: Original = 800,000.
Remember to divide by the original, 800,000.

methods.title: Reverse percentage
methods.example: After a 15% discount, a television costs $340. What was the original price?
steps: A 15% discount uses the multiplier 0.85, so original × 0.85 = 340.
Reverse it: original = 340 ÷ 0.85 = $400.
Check forwards: $400 × 0.85 = $340.
Correct.

methods.title: Simple interest
methods.example: Zahra invests a principal of $500 at 4% simple interest for 2 years. Find the interest and the total amount.
steps: Total amount = principal + interest = 500 + 40 = $540.
Check by recalculating: 4% of 500 is 20, and two years of that is 40, confirming the interest.

workedExamples.title: Percentage of an amount
workedExamples.solution: Use the decimal method. 12% = 0.12, so 0.12 × 250 = 30 shillings. As a check with building blocks: 10% of 250 = 25, and 2% is one fifth of that, 5, giving 25 + 5 = 30. Both agree.

workedExamples.title: Increase with a multiplier
workedExamples.solution: An 8% increase uses the multiplier 1.08. So $450 × 1.08 = $486. Check by parts: 8% of 450 = 36, and 450 + 36 = 486. Correct.

workedExamples.title: Decrease with a multiplier
workedExamples.solution: A 12% decrease uses the multiplier 0.88 (because 100% − 12% = 88%). So 350 × 0.88 = 308 kg. Check by parts: 12% of 350 = 42, and 350 − 42 = 308. Correct.

workedExamples.title: Percentage change
workedExamples.prompt: A shopkeeper's weekly revenue rises from $800,000 to $920,000. Find the percentage increase.
workedExamples.solution: Change = 920,000 − 800,000 = 120,000. Original = 800,000. Percentage increase = (120,000 ÷ 800,000) × 100% = 0.15 × 100% = 15%. Remember to divide by the original, 800,000.

workedExamples.title: Reverse percentage
workedExamples.prompt: After a 15% discount, a television costs $340. What was the original price?
workedExamples.solution: A 15% discount uses the multiplier 0.85, so original × 0.85 = 340. Reverse it: original = 340 ÷ 0.85 = $400. Check forwards: $400 × 0.85 = $340. Correct.

workedExamples.title: Simple interest
workedExamples.prompt: Zahra invests a principal of $500 at 4% simple interest for 2 years. Find the interest and the total amount.
workedExamples.solution: Interest = P × R × T = 500 × 0.04 × 2 = $40. Total amount = principal + interest = 500 + 40 = $540.

workedExamples.title: Percentage profit
workedExamples.prompt: Idris buys a goat for $40 and sells it for $52. Find the percentage profit.
workedExamples.solution: Profit = 52 − 40 = $12. Percentage profit = (profit ÷ cost price) × 100% = (12 ÷ 40) × 100% = 30%. We divide by the cost price, 40.

workedExamples.title: Combined discount and tax
workedExamples.prompt: A jacket costs $120. A 25% discount is applied, then 8% tax is added on the discounted price. Find the final cost.
workedExamples.solution: Discount multiplier 0.75, tax multiplier 1.08. Final cost = 120 × 0.75 × 1.08 = 90 × 1.08 = $97.20. Doing both steps as one line of multipliers is quick and reliable.

workedExamples.title: Reverse from a total
workedExamples.prompt: A savings account grows to $920 after one year of simple interest at 15%. What was the principal?
workedExamples.solution: One year at 15% multiplies the principal by 1.15 (the principal is kept and 15% interest is added). So principal × 1.15 = 920, giving principal = 920 ÷ 1.15 = $800. Check: $800 interest at 15% = $120, and 800 + 120 = $920. Correct.

workedExamples.title: Practice 10
workedExamples.prompt: A trader buys goods for $50 and sells for $65. Find the percentage profit.
workedExamples.solution: Profit = 65 − 50 = $15. Percentage profit = (profit ÷ cost price) × 100% = (15 ÷ 50) × 100% = 30%. We divide by the cost price, $50.

workedExamples.title: Practice 11
workedExamples.prompt: A restaurant bill is $65 with an 18% tip. Find the total using a multiplier.
workedExamples.solution: An 18% tip uses the multiplier 1.18. So $65 × 1.18 = $76.70. Check by parts: 18% of 65 = 11.70, and 65 + 11.70 = 76.70. Correct.

workedExamples.title: Practice 12
workedExamples.prompt: After a 20% increase, a salary is $48,000. Find the original salary.

activities.title: Market Discount Detective
activities.materials: a notebook, a pen, and some real shop or market prices (from a visit, a receipt, or an advertisement).
steps: Collect five items with their original prices and a discount percentage for each.
For each item, work out the multiplier (for example, 30% off means ×0.70).
Calculate the sale price and the money saved for every item.
Rank the deals from the biggest saving to the smallest. Which discount saved the most shillings?
Write one sentence explaining why a bigger percentage does not always mean a bigger saving in shillings.

activities.title: The Savings Growth Game
steps: Imagine you save a principal of $1,000 at 5% simple interest.
Make a table with columns for Year, Interest that year, and Total so far.
Fill in the total for years 1 to 5. With simple interest, the same interest is added each year.
Now try a rate of 8% and compare. How much more do you earn over five years?
Discuss with your family: why does a higher interest rate matter so much for long-term saving?

activities.title: Family Trade Investigation
activities.materials: a family member who buys and sells anything (food, livestock, goods), or an imagined trade.
steps: Choose an item with a cost price and a selling price (for example, a goat bought for $40 and sold for $52).
Work out the profit or loss in dollars or shillings.
Turn it into a percentage profit or loss on the cost price.
Try three different selling prices and see how the percentage profit changes.
Decide the lowest selling price that still gives at least a 20% profit.

activities.title: Percentage Claim Fact-Check
activities.materials: a newspaper, a radio advert you remember, or a product label.
steps: Find three claims that use a percentage, such as 50% more free or prices cut by 30%.
For each claim, work out what the number really means with an example amount.
Ask: is the claim clear, or could it mislead a shopper? What is missing?
Write a short consumer tip explaining how to check a percentage claim before believing it.
Being able to question percentage claims protects you and your family from being misled.

activities.title: Reverse Percentage Puzzle Maker
activities.materials: paper and pen, and a partner to challenge (or your AI tutor if no partner is available).
steps: Secretly choose an original price and a percentage discount.
Work out the sale price using the multiplier.
Give your partner (or your AI tutor) only the sale price and the discount, and ask them to find the original.
Check their answer against your secret original. Swap roles and repeat.
Make the puzzles harder by using a discount and then a tax, both as multipliers.

activities.title: Budget Percentages (Family Task)
activities.materials: an imagined monthly income, such as $2,000, and paper.
steps: Split the income into percentages: for example housing 30%, food 20%, transport 15%, savings 10%, other 25%.
Check your percentages add up to 100%.
Work out the amount in dollars for each part of the budget.
Set aside the savings portion and calculate one year of simple interest on it at 5%.
Discuss with your family which percentages you might change, and why.

After a 15% discount, a TV costs $340. Find the original price.

reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Trade is at the heart of daily life, from the camel markets of Garissa to the shops of Eastleigh. Anyone who buys goods to sell them again needs to understand profit and loss. The cost price is what an item cost to buy or make; the selling price is what it is sold for. If the selling price is higher, there is a profit; if it is lower, there is a loss. To express profit or loss as a percentage, we use our percentage-change idea, and by convention we compare against the cost price:
